evidence.claim: The byway council’s plan describes a landscape shared by all four towns: each lies within the Piscataquog watershed, and the river winds through three of them.
evidence.quote: The Piscataquog River winds through three of the four communities of the byway and all four communities are part of the Piscataquog River watershed.

evidence.claim: The byway began as a public planning effort in January 2007. A public tour followed that May, and the State Byways Council and state transportation department approved the designation in June 2008.

evidence.claim: A local council organized the following month to develop its management plan.
evidence.quote: July 2008: A local Byway Council was organized and its first meeting was held to gather components for development of a Corridor Management Plan.

evidence.claim: The route’s namesake connects several stops: John Stark spent time at the Page homestead in Dunbarton, while New Boston received the cannon named for his wife, Molly.
evidence.quote: During the time between the French and Indian Wars and the Revolutionary War, General Stark spent much time at the Page homestead in Dunbarton

evidence.claim: New Boston received the cannon named for his wife, Molly.
evidence.quote: The 1743 cannon, which appears on the town seal, was given by General John Stark to the New Boston Artillery Company after the Battle of Bennington.

evidence.claim: the cannon named for his wife, Molly.
evidence.quote: The cannon that was captured from the British during the Battle of the Bennington is named for General John Stark’s wife, Molly Stark.

evidence.claim: By 2008, sections of former railroad bed in Weare, New Boston and Goffstown had become walking and cycling paths.
evidence.quote: Sections of the old railroad bed through the towns of Weare, New Boston and Goffstown are now walking and biking paths.

evidence.claim: From Weare, follow NH 114 and NH 77 south to New Boston, then NH 13 toward Goffstown along the river.
evidence.quote: along NH 13 from Goffstown’s downtown west to New Boston, north along NH 77 and NH 114 to Weare, east along NH 77 to Dunbarton, and south along NH 13 back to Goffstown

evidence.claim: Continue north on NH 13 to Dunbarton and return west on NH 77 to Weare, completing the four-town circuit.
evidence.quote: east along NH 77 to Dunbarton, and south along NH 13 back to Goffstown

evidence.claim: The Pine Tree Riot began with a dispute over timber reserved for Royal Navy masts.
evidence.quote: In 1722, under the Broad Arrow Policy it became illegal to cut down white pine trees larger than 12 inches in diameter in New Hampshire in order to reserve them for use as Royal Navy masts.

evidence.claim: The 1722 rule prohibited cutting white pines more than twelve inches in diameter in New Hampshire.
evidence.quote: In 1722, under the Broad Arrow Policy it became illegal to cut down white pine trees larger than 12 inches in diameter in New Hampshire

evidence.claim: In April 1772, Sheriff Benjamin Whiting and Deputy John Quigley went to South Weare to arrest mill-owner leader Ebenezer Mudgett.
evidence.quote: On April 13, 1772, Benjamin Whiting, Sheriff of Hillsborough County, and his Deputy John Quigley were sent to South Weare with a warrant to arrest the leader of the Weare mill owners, Ebenezer Mudgett.

evidence.claim: The following morning, Mudgett and other townsmen assaulted both officers at the inn where they were staying and forced them out of town.
evidence.quote: The next day, Mudgett and twenty men attacked the Sheriff and Deputy at the Quimby Inn, beating them nearly to death with large rods and sending them out of town on horseback.

evidence.claim: Eight men faced charges. They pleaded guilty, and the court imposed fines of twenty shillings each plus hearing costs.
evidence.quote: The rioters pleaded guilty, and the judges fined them 20 shillings each and ordered them to pay the cost of the court hearing.

evidence.claim: Eight men faced charges.
evidence.quote: Eight men were ordered to post bail and appear in court

evidence.claim: The covered railroad bridge is gone; its concrete-capped granite abutments remain beside the Piscataquog River.
evidence.quote: on granite slab abutments that are still visible, capped in concrete.

evidence.claim: The Boston and Maine Railroad built the bridge in 1901, replacing an earlier crossing built by the New Hampshire Central Railroad in 1850.
evidence.quote: It was built in 1901 by the Boston and Maine Railroad, on the site of an earlier bridge built in 1850 by the New Hampshire Central Railroad

evidence.claim: It entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1975, but arson destroyed it the next year.
evidence.quote: The bridge was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975. It was destroyed by arson in 1976

evidence.claim: The railroad chose not to replace it. The surviving abutments lie just east of the Main Street road bridge.
evidence.quote: the railroad decided not to replace the bridge.

evidence.claim: The surviving abutments lie just east of the Main Street road bridge.

evidence.claim: Freight service continued east of the river until September 1980; complete abandonment of the line followed in February 1981.
evidence.quote: Freight service still ran on the line east of the river until September 20, 1980, with total abandonment following in February 1981.

evidence.claim: Granite abutments capped in concrete mark the former railroad crossing.

evidence.claim: Dunbarton once carried the name Starkstown. Granted under that name in 1748, it became Dunbarton when incorporated in 1765, taking its name from the Scottish home of settler Archibald Stark.
evidence.quote: Originally granted as "Gorham's-town" in 1735, and re-granted as "Starkstown" in 1748, the town was incorporated in 1765 as Dunbarton. The name came from Dunbartonshire in Scotland, hometown to Archibald Stark, a prominent settler.

evidence.claim: John Stark spent time at the Page homestead between the French and Indian Wars and the Revolutionary War, and married Elizabeth “Molly” Page.
evidence.quote: During the time between the French and Indian Wars and the Revolutionary War, General Stark spent much time at the Page homestead in Dunbarton, and later married Elizabeth “Molly” Page.

evidence.claim: The 2008 byway plan included the homestead and a statue honoring his son Caleb, who also fought in the Revolutionary War.
evidence.quote: The Caleb Stark Statue in Dunbarton stands as a tribute to General John Stark’s son who also fought in the Revolutionary war.

evidence.claim: The 2008 byway plan included the homestead
evidence.quote: The homestead still stands today, and is one of the featured historic sites along the route.

evidence.claim: The plan placed Caleb’s statue on the town common along Stark Highway North, among the town’s historic sites.

flags: Loop follows supplied strip order beginning in Weare, reversing the current draft’s direction: Weare, New Boston, Goffstown, Dunbarton, then Weare.
Current riot text conflated discovery of illegal logs with the sheriff’s arrest visit; revised to the detailed chronology. Removed exact twenty attackers because the article gives conflicting counts.

The 2008 plan calls Bennington a 1776 battle in the body but 1777 in its footnote. Battle year omitted. No claim that national or All-American Road designation was granted: the plan records only an application.
Historic-property and road-condition evidence in the corridor plan is from 2008. No present access to the Page homestead, current bus-turn warning, or visitor hours are asserted.
The plan places the route entirely in Hillsborough County, while the Dunbarton article locates that town in Merrimack County. County-wide claim omitted.
Cannon firing is described as an ongoing annual practice, not a verified 2026 event schedule. The source says 1743 cannon; current cast wording was narrowed to dating to 1743.
